claim: Spirochete bacteria exhibit a distinctive means of swimming via undulations of the entire cell.
source: Spirochete bacteria, including important pathogens, exhibit a distinctive means of swimming via undulations of the entire cell.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing a characteristic of spirochete bacteria.

claim: Motility in spirochetes is powered by the rotation of supercoiled 'endoflagella' that wrap around the cell body, confined within the periplasmic space.
source: Motility is powered by the rotation of supercoiled 'endoflagella' that wrap around the cell body, confined within the periplasmic space.
evidence: This statement describes the mechanism of motility in spirochetes based on established knowledge.

claim: Leptospira flagellar filaments are coated by a highly asymmetric, multi-component sheath layer.
source: We show that these filaments are coated by a highly asymmetric, multi-component sheath layer, contrasting with flagellin-only homopolymers previously observed in exoflagellated bacteria.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Leptospira flagellar filaments contrast with flagellin-only homopolymers previously observed in exoflagellated bacteria.
source: We show that these filaments are coated by a highly asymmetric, multi-component sheath layer, contrasting with flagellin-only homopolymers previously observed in exoflagellated bacteria.
evidence: This comparison is made based on prior knowledge of exoflagellated bacteria and the current findings.

claim: Distinct sheath proteins localize to the filament inner and outer curvatures to define the supercoiling geometry.
source: Distinct sheath proteins localize to the filament inner and outer curvatures to define the supercoiling geometry, explaining a key functional attribute of this spirochete flagellum.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis and modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spirochetes have powerful swimming capabilities that enable them to rapidly disseminate through connective tissue, blood, and organs.
source: Spirochetes have powerful swimming capabilities that enable them to rapidly disseminate through connective tissue, blood, and organs (Wunder et al., 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The unique configuration of the flagellum in spirochetes allows them to 'drill' through highly viscous media.
source: This swimming capability is enabled by a unique configuration of the flagellum in these organisms (Charon et al., 2012; Li et al., 2000a; Wolgemuth et al., 2006; Figure 1A), which allows them to 'drill' through highly viscous media (Li et al., 2000b; Wolgemuth et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: By housing their flagella in the periplasm, spirochetes protect these filaments from environmental insults, such as immune surveillance.
source: By housing their flagella in the periplasm, spirochetes protect these filaments from environmental insults, such as immune surveillance (Vernel-Pauillac and Werts, 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A similar function to periplasmic flagella may be achieved by the membranous sheath that coats the exoflagellum in Vibrio cholerae.
source: (a similar function may be achieved by the membranous sheath that coats the exoflagellum in Vibrio cholerae Yoon and Mekalanos, 2008).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by a citation.

claim: Spirochetal flagella exhibit supercoiled architectures.
source: Spirochetal flagella exhibit supercoiled architectures (Charon et al., 1992; Dombrowski et al., 2009)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Supercoiled architectures in spirochetal flagella have been linked to productive motility.
source: Spirochetal flagella exhibit supercoiled architectures (Charon et al., 1992; Dombrowski et al., 2009), which have been linked to productive motility (Wolgemuth, 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Amongst pathogenic spirochete species, supercoiled flagellar architectures have been linked to virulence.
source: Spirochetal flagella exhibit supercoiled architectures (Charon et al., 1992; Dombrowski et al., 2009), which have been linked to productive motility (Wolgemuth, 2015), and amongst pathogenic species, to virulence (Ko et al., 2009; McBride et al., 2005; Sultan et al., 2013; Wunder et al., 2016a).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Leptospira spp. includes pathogenic species that cause human and animal disease, as well as free-living saprophytic species.
source: Leptospira spp. includes pathogenic species that cause human and animal disease, as well as free-living saprophytic species (Picardeau, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Leptospira possess flagellar filaments that spontaneously curl into tightly supercoiled shapes when isolated, following nearly coplanar paths.
source: Unique among known bacteria, including spirochetes, Leptospira possess flagellar filaments that spontaneously curl into tightly supercoiled shapes when isolated, following nearly coplanar paths (Bromley and Charon, 1979; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reference to a figure showing the supercoiled morphology.

claim: The flagellar filament superposes a curved path on the underlying helical body, resulting in overall 'spiral' or 'hook' cell end shapes depending on the motor rotation direction.
source: The flagellar filament superposes a curved path on the underlying helical body, resulting in overall 'spiral' or 'hook' cell end shapes depending on the motor rotation direction (Charon and Goldstein, 2002; Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reference to a figure.

claim: Leptospira cells travel rapidly and unidirectionally when flagellar motors at opposing ends of the organism rotate in opposite directions.
source: Similar to other spirochetes, Leptospira cells travel rapidly and unidirectionally when flagellar motors at opposing ends of the organism rotate in opposite directions (i.e. counterclockwise vs. clockwise when viewing the motor from the cell exterior), but stall when the motors are both rotating in the same direction (Goldstein and Charon, 1988; Wolgemuth, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Leptospira cells stall when the motors are both rotating in the same direction.
source: Similar to other spirochetes, Leptospira cells travel rapidly and unidirectionally when flagellar motors at opposing ends of the organism rotate in opposite directions (i.e. counterclockwise vs. clockwise when viewing the motor from the cell exterior), but stall when the motors are both rotating in the same direction (Goldstein and Charon, 1988; Wolgemuth, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Leptospira can adopt a distinct 'crawling' mode while bound to surfaces.
source: Leptospira can also adopt a distinct 'crawling' mode while bound to surfaces (Tahara et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Leptospira have a complex flagellar composition compared to exoflagellated bacteria.
source: As with all spirochetes, Leptospira have a complex flagellar composition compared to exoflagellated bacteria (Charon and Goldstein, 2002; Figure 1B; Table 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and references to figures and a table.

claim: Flagellar filaments from non-spirochete bacteria generally have a single protein component (flagellin).
source: Flagellar filaments from non-spirochete bacteria generally have a single protein component (Erhardt et al., 2010) (flagellin).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Spirochetal flagellar filaments are comprised of a flagellin homolog (FlaB) and FlaA, a second and completely unrelated component.
source: In contrast, spirochetal flagellar filaments are comprised of a flagellin homolog (FlaB) and FlaA (Brahamsha and Greenberg, 1988), a second and completely unrelated component.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: FlaA and FlaB proteins can occur in multiple isoforms within a single organism.
source: FlaA and FlaB proteins can occur in multiple isoforms within a single organism (Wolgemuth et al., 2006; Table 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and reference to a table.

claim: Deletion of FlaA in Leptospira affects flagellar curvature and diminishes motility and pathogenicity.
source: Deletion of FlaA or FlaB in Leptospira leads to distinct phenotypes: deletion of FlaA affects flagellar curvature and diminishes motility and pathogenicity (Lambert et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Deletion of FlaB in Leptospira eliminates the filament entirely.
source: deletion of FlaB eliminates the filament entirely (Picardeau et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Similar observations regarding FlaA and FlaB deletions have been made in other spirochetes.
source: Similar observations have been made in other spirochetes (Li et al., 2000a; Motaleb et al., 2000)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Structural and functional adaptations in Leptospira flagella may be relevant to spirochetes as a whole.
source: Similar observations have been made in other spirochetes (Li et al., 2000a; Motaleb et al., 2000), indicating that structural and functional adaptations in Leptospira flagella may be relevant to spirochetes as a whole.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of observations across spirochete species.

claim: FcpA and FcpB are Leptospira-specific components of the flagellum.
source: Recently, two novel Leptospira-specific components of the flagellum, FcpA and FcpB (Table 1), were identified whose deletion abolishes the ability of flagella to assume their characteristic supercoiled form and dramatically reduces motility and virulence (Wunder et al., 2016a; Wunder et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and reference to a table.

claim: Deletion of FcpA or FcpB abolishes the ability of flagella to assume their characteristic supercoiled form.
source: Recently, two novel Leptospira-specific components of the flagellum, FcpA and FcpB (Table 1), were identified whose deletion abolishes the ability of flagella to assume their characteristic supercoiled form and dramatically reduces motility and virulence (Wunder et al., 2016a; Wunder et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Deletion of FcpA or FcpB dramatically reduces motility and virulence in Leptospira.
source: Recently, two novel Leptospira-specific components of the flagellum, FcpA and FcpB (Table 1), were identified whose deletion abolishes the ability of flagella to assume their characteristic supercoiled form and dramatically reduces motility and virulence (Wunder et al., 2016a; Wunder et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: FcpA from L. biflexa adopts a unique fold unrelated to globular domains found in available flagellin structures.
source: Using X-ray crystallography, we established that the flagellar sheath components FcpA and FcpB adopt unique folds, unrelated to globular domains found in available flagellin structures (Figure 1C–F; Galkin et al., 2008; Samatey et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the X-ray crystallography analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: FcpB from L. interrogans adopts a unique fold unrelated to globular domains found in available flagellin structures.
source: Using X-ray crystallography, we established that the flagellar sheath components FcpA and FcpB adopt unique folds, unrelated to globular domains found in available flagellin structures (Figure 1C–F; Galkin et al., 2008; Samatey et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the X-ray crystallography analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: FcpA from L. biflexa was crystallized in three different space groups.
source: FcpA from L. biflexa was crystallized in three different space groups (San Martin et al., 2017; Table 2)
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by a citation and reference to a table.

claim: The 3D fold of FcpA is previously unseen within the PDB (release July 2019).
source: FcpA from L. biflexa was crystallized in three different space groups (San Martin et al., 2017; Table 2), revealing a 3D fold previously unseen within the PDB (release July 2019) as reported by several structural alignment algorithms (Holm and Laakso, 2016; Madej et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to structural alignment algorithms.

claim: FcpB from L. interrogans was crystallized in the orthorhombic space group P212121.
source: FcpB from the pathogenic species, L. interrogans (ortholog of the L. biflexa protein; Table 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), was crystallized in the orthorhombic space group P212121 (Table 2).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by reference to a table.

claim: The fold of FcpB exhibits distant structural homology to proteins of the Mam33 family, including human mitochondrial protein p32.
source: The resulting fold exhibits distant structural homology to proteins of the Mam33 family, including human mitochondrial protein p32 (Jiang et al., 1999) that exhibit affinity for a number of protein partners.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Homology to FcpB was also detected with VC1805, a protein from Vibrio cholerae that can bind complement protein C1q.
source: Homology to FcpB was also detected with VC1805 (Sheikh et al., 2008), a protein from Vibrio cholerae that can bind complement protein C1q.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: FcpA and FcpB are highly distinct in overall size and shape.
source: FcpA and FcpB are highly distinct in overall size and shape.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis.

claim: FcpA assumes an all-helical fold consisting of a twisted stack of eleven α-helices, arranged in a 'V'-shaped architecture with arms of unequal length.
source: FcpA assumes an all-helical fold consisting of a twisted stack of eleven α-helices, arranged in a 'V'-shaped architecture with arms of unequal length (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in the figure.

claim: FcpB adopts a wide and flat oblong shape, consisting of an 8-stranded anti-parallel β-sheet with two long α-helices packed on one side.
source: In contrast to FcpA, FcpB adopts a wide and flat oblong shape, consisting of an 8-stranded anti-parallel β-sheet with two long α-helices (α1 and α4) packed on one side (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The strongly curved supercoiling geometry of intact Leptospira flagellar filaments precluded the use of most structure determination methods, including cryo-EM single-particle 3D reconstruction.
source: The strongly curved supercoiling geometry of intact Leptospira flagellar filaments (Figure 2A) precluded the use of most structure determination methods, including cryo-EM single-particle 3D reconstruction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Methods)
evidence: This is a methodological observation explaining the choice of cryo-tomography.

claim: A total of ~10,800 sub-volumes were input into a customized sub-tomogram alignment procedure.
source: A total of ~10,800 sub-volumes were input into a customized sub-tomogram alignment procedure (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the data processing.

claim: The resulting averaged map achieved an overall (average) resolution of ~10 Å.
source: The resulting averaged map achieved an overall (average) resolution of ~10 Å (Figure 2B–E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a primary result from the sub-tomogram averaging analysis.

claim: The averaged map exhibits a series of concentric protein layers centered around a ~ 2 nm central pore.
source: The resulting averaged map achieved an overall (average) resolution of ~10 Å (Figure 2B–E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and exhibits a series of concentric protein layers centered around a ~ 2 nm central pore (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is a direct observation from the averaged map shown in the figure.

claim: The averaged map exhibits a distinct array of globular features decorating the filament surface.
source: The resulting averaged map achieved an overall (average) resolution of ~10 Å (Figure 2B–E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and exhibits a series of concentric protein layers centered around a ~ 2 nm central pore (Figure 2F), as well as a distinct array of globular features decorating the filament surface (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the averaged map shown in the figure.

claim: The morphology of the inner two density layers closely resembles that of the helically assembled flagellin domains D0 and D1 of filaments from exoflagellated bacteria.
source: The morphology of the inner two density layers (Figure 2G) closely resembles that of the helically assembled flagellin domains D0 and D1 of filaments from exoflagellated bacteria (Wang et al., 2017; Yonekura et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The structural homology of the inner two density layers is consistent with earlier predictions that the core of the spirochete filament is composed of FlaB.
source: This structural homology is consistent with earlier predictions that the core of the spirochete filament is composed of FlaB (Li et al., 2008; Nauman et al., 1969), a protein that lacks the D2 and D3 domains present in flagellins from many exoflagellated bacteria (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural homology and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: FlaB is a protein that lacks the D2 and D3 domains present in flagellins from many exoflagellated bacteria.
source: This structural homology is consistent with earlier predictions that the core of the spirochete filament is composed of FlaB (Li et al., 2008; Nauman et al., 1969), a protein that lacks the D2 and D3 domains present in flagellins from many exoflagellated bacteria (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the domain composition of FlaB supported by a figure.

claim: Sheath densities were mainly localized on the outer curvature of the filament, or 'convex' side.
source: Sheath densities were mainly localized on the outer curvature of the filament, or 'convex' side, thus offsetting the filament center of mass away from the central pore when the filament is viewed in cross section (Figure 2C,F, Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tomographic map shown in the figure.

claim: The asymmetric sheath localization offsets the filament center of mass away from the central pore when the filament is viewed in cross section.
source: Sheath densities were mainly localized on the outer curvature of the filament, or 'convex' side, thus offsetting the filament center of mass away from the central pore when the filament is viewed in cross section (Figure 2C,F, Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tomographic map shown in the figure.

claim: The break in helical subunit arrangement in the Leptospira endoflagellum sharply contrasts with symmetric structures observed for exoflagella from Salmonella, Campylobacter, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Bacillus subtilis.
source: This break in helical subunit arrangement in the Leptospira endoflagellum sharply contrasts with symmetric structures which were previously observed for exoflagella from Salmonella (Sasaki et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017; Yonekura et al., 2003), Campylobacter (Galkin et al., 2008), Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Bacillus subtilis (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Two independent docking strategies were used to fit FcpA and FcpB molecular envelopes into the reconstructed filament map.
source: We used two independent docking strategies to fit FcpA and FcpB molecular envelopes into the reconstructed filament map (see Materials and methods)
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the approach used.

claim: FcpA and FcpB were identified at convergent locations distributed across the convex side of the sheath region.
source: We used two independent docking strategies to fit FcpA and FcpB molecular envelopes into the reconstructed filament map (see Materials and methods) and identified convergent locations for these two proteins that were distributed across the convex side of the sheath region (Figure 3, Video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the docking analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The sheath sites form an array of globular features that closely follows the canonical 11-protofilament helical lattice identified in flagellar filaments of Salmonella and other non-spirochete bacteria.
source: These sheath sites form an array of globular features that closely follows the canonical 11-protofilament helical lattice identified in flagellar filaments of Salmonella and other non-spirochete bacteria (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Six adjacent, curved rows of 'V'-shaped density profiles form an interlocking array for FcpA.
source: For FcpA, six adjacent, curved rows of 'V'-shaped density profiles form an interlocking array (Figure 4; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The FcpB sites were resolved as four adjacent rows of flattened density lobes protruding slightly outward from the FcpA portion of the sheath.
source: The FcpB sites were resolved as four adjacent rows of flattened density lobes protruding slightly outward from the FcpA portion of the sheath (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The resulting assembly consists of an inner layer of FcpA molecules in close contact with the FlaB core, and an outer layer of FcpB molecules nestled between rows of FcpA.
source: The resulting assembly consists of an inner layer of FcpA molecules in close contact with the FlaB core, and an outer layer of FcpB molecules nestled between rows of FcpA (Video 2).
evidence: This is a summary of the structural arrangement observed in the analysis.

claim: The asymmetric localization of FcpA and FcpB on the convex side of the sheath is consistent with prior flagellum electron-microscopic imaging studies performed with antibody labels.
source: The asymmetric localization of FcpA and FcpB, specifically on the convex side of the sheath, is distinct from previously characterized exoflagella but is consistent with prior flagellum electron-microscopic imaging studies performed with antibody labels (Wunder et al., 2016a; Wunder et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The localization of FcpB sites were validated by comparison with a reconstruction of filaments from an fcpB- mutant.
source: The localization of FcpB sites were further validated by comparison with a similar reconstruction of filaments from an fcpB- mutant (Figure 2I), for which the projected cross-section of the fcpB- map was missing four globular features found in the wild-type map (Figure 2H) that coincide with our FcpB docking solutions.
evidence: This is a validation of the FcpB localization using mutant data shown in the figure.

claim: The filaments from imaged fcpA- mutants were significantly smaller in diameter than filaments from wild-type and fcpB- mutants.
source: However, the filaments from imaged fcpA- mutants were significantly smaller in diameter than filaments from wild-type and fcpB- mutants (see the last Results section, below)
evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging data.

claim: Filaments from the fcpA- mutant have lost FcpA and FcpB.
source: However, the filaments from imaged fcpA- mutants were significantly smaller in diameter than filaments from wild-type and fcpB- mutants (see the last Results section, below), indicating that filaments from the fcpA- mutant have lost FcpA and FcpB, in agreement with previous findings (Wunder et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the diameter measurements and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Additional sheath features are found on the filament concave side, manifesting as two rows of elongated density units, separated by a groove that exposes the core.
source: Additional sheath features are found on the filament concave side, highly divergent from the ones observed on the convex face. These inner-side elements manifested as two rows of elongated density units, separated by a groove that exposes the core (Figures 2C and 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the tomographic map shown in the figure.

claim: FlaA is presumed to reside in the spirochete sheath.
source: FlaA is also presumed to reside in the spirochete sheath (Li et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Comparing the fcpB– map with the wild-type map, a missing mass within the concave sheath region suggests candidate positions for FlaA1 and FlaA2.
source: FlaA is also presumed to reside in the spirochete sheath (Li et al., 2008), and comparing the fcpB– map with the wild-type map, a missing mass within the concave sheath region indeed suggests candidate positions for FlaA1 and FlaA2 (Figure 2I, red asterisk).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of wild-type and mutant maps shown in the figure.

claim: Additional averaging of the map core region revealed homology with flagellar filaments from Salmonella and other exoflagellates.
source: Additional averaging of the map core region revealed homology with flagellar filaments from Salmonella and other exoflagellates (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis supported by a citation.

claim: A strongly preferred filament orientation in the specimen ice layer resulted in a 'missing wedge' of Fourier-space data characteristic of cryo-tomography.
source: Due to a strongly preferred filament orientation in the specimen ice layer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), the potential effect of a 'missing wedge' of Fourier-space data characteristic of the cryo-tomography (Carazo et al., 2006) could not be fully eliminated.
evidence: This is a methodological observation explaining a limitation of the data.

claim: 3D auto-correlation analysis within the core region detected a signal corresponding to the 11-fold helical symmetry operator present in previously determined flagellar structures.
source: By performing 3D auto-correlation analysis within the core region, however, we detected a signal corresponding to the 11-fold helical symmetry operator present in previously determined flagellar structures (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The 11-fold symmetry operator is mostly congruent with the observed lattice positions of FcpA and FcpB molecules identified in the sheath.
source: The 11-fold symmetry operator is mostly congruent with the observed lattice positions of FcpA and FcpB molecules identified in the sheath (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), although there are minor deviations due to filament curvature.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis shown in the figure.

claim: After applying 11-fold averaging using the symmetry operator, additional features were resolved in the core region, including some α-helices.
source: After applying 11-fold averaging using the symmetry operator, additional features were resolved in the core region, including some α-helices, and revealed a structural homology with the D0/D1 region of the Salmonella flagellum (Figure 3B,C; Figure 3—figure supplement 6; Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The resulting filament atomic model exhibits a consistent set of interactions between FcpA and the FlaB core.
source: The resulting filament atomic model exhibits a consistent set of interactions between FcpA and the FlaB core, reflecting the approximate helical symmetry of fitted components (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the atomic model shown in the figure.

claim: FcpA molecules project both arms toward the core region, positioning the long arm within contact radius of two predicted loop regions in FlaB.
source: FcpA molecules project both arms toward the core region, positioning the long arm within contact radius of two predicted loop regions in FlaB (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the atomic model shown in the figure.

claim: The FcpA α3-α4 hairpin surface that forms crystal lattice contacts in all three FcpA X-ray structures is buried in the interactions with FlaB.
source: Such interactions bury the same protein surface of the FcpA α3-α4 hairpin that forms crystal lattice contacts in all three FcpA X-ray structures.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the crystal structures with the filament model.

claim: FlaB loop regions engaged in interactions with FcpA project outwards from the core surface toward the predicted FcpA arm positions.
source: The FlaB loop regions engaged in these interactions project outwards from the core surface toward the predicted FcpA arm positions.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the atomic model.

claim: FlaB loops in Leptospira (both 6–7 residues in length) likely contribute to the functional interface between FcpA and the core.
source: Thus, FlaB loops in Leptospira (both 6–7 residues in length) likely contribute to the functional interface between FcpA and the core.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Modeled FcpB subunits project their central β-sheets radially away from the core.
source: Modeled FcpB subunits project their central β-sheets radially away from the core and present several elements within contact radius of the FcpA inner sheath layer, including one of the long FcpB α-helices (α4) as well as several loops located at the proximal edge of the β-sheet (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the atomic model shown in the figure.

claim: Two highly conserved surface patches on FcpB are in close proximity with nearby FcpA molecules.
source: We identified two highly conserved surface patches on FcpB which are in close proximity with nearby FcpA molecules (Figure 4E), suggesting that these sites may mediate direct interactions between FcpA and FcpB.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the atomic model shown in the figure.

claim: The conserved surface patches on FcpB may mediate direct interactions between FcpA and FcpB.
source: We identified two highly conserved surface patches on FcpB which are in close proximity with nearby FcpA molecules (Figure 4E), suggesting that these sites may mediate direct interactions between FcpA and FcpB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: The corresponding FcpA surface interaction regions predicted by the model are also conserved.
source: The corresponding FcpA surface interaction regions predicted by our model are also conserved, and largely match a conserved protein:protein interface found in all FcpA crystal forms.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the atomic model and crystal structures.

claim: Complementary electrostatic potentials map onto the FcpA:FcpB interface.
source: Complementary electrostatic potentials also map onto the FcpA:FcpB interface (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The modeled FcpB sites are too far away from the core to make direct contact.
source: The modeled FcpB sites are too far away from the core to make direct contact, providing an explanation for why deletion of FcpA leads to concurrent loss of FcpB from the filament (Wunder et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the atomic model and supported by a citation.

claim: Deletion of FcpA leads to concurrent loss of FcpB from the filament.
source: The modeled FcpB sites are too far away from the core to make direct contact, providing an explanation for why deletion of FcpA leads to concurrent loss of FcpB from the filament (Wunder et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The wild-type filament map provides evidence of contact between FcpA and unassigned elements within the concave sheath region.
source: The wild-type filament map provides evidence of contact between FcpA and unassigned elements within the concave sheath region, particularly on one side of the groove (Figure 3A; bottom left corner).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the map shown in the figure.

claim: FcpA may interact directly with one or both FlaA isoforms.
source: Since the unassigned material in the concave sheath region is likely composed of FlaA1 and/or FlaA2, FcpA may interact directly with one or both FlaA isoforms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Pull-down assays of purified L. biflexa flagellar filaments identified interactions between FcpA and FlaA2.
source: Indeed, pull-down assays of purified L. biflexa flagellar filaments recently identified interactions between FcpA and FlaA2 (Sasaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Trajectory analysis of aligned filament subtomograms from wild-type, fcpA– and fcpB– samples reveals a progressive straightening in isolated flagellar filaments as sheath components are lost.
source: Trajectory analysis of aligned filament subtomograms from wild-type, fcpA– and fcpB– samples reveals a progressive straightening in isolated flagellar filaments as sheath components are lost (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the trajectory analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The observation of progressive straightening supports and extends previous reports associating fcpA and fcpB mutations with loss of filament curvature together with pronounced functional effects.
source: This observation supports and extends previous reports associating these mutations with loss of filament curvature together with pronounced functional effects (Wunder et al., 2016a; Wunder et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Wild-type filament segments almost exclusively fall within a single peak in the measured curvature distribution, centered at the average value (~5 µm−1; 0.2 µm radius of curvature).
source: Wild-type filament segments almost exclusively fall within a single peak in the measured curvature distribution, centered at the average value (~5 µm−1; 0.2 µm radius of curvature; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the curvature analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Mutant fcpB– filament segments show a mixed population of curvatures, with only ~50% of segments falling within the wild-type peak.
source: In contrast, mutant fcpB– filament segments (which still contain FcpA Wunder et al., 2018) show a mixed population of curvatures, with only ~50% of segments falling within the wild-type peak, while curvature for most of the remaining segments is estimated at 3 µm−1 or less (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the curvature analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Curvature is further reduced in fcpA– filaments, which lack both FcpA and FcpB.
source: Curvature is further reduced in fcpA– filaments, which lack both FcpA and FcpB (Wunder et al., 2018): only a vestigial population of segments exhibit the wild-type curvature, while the estimated curvature of most segments is again below 3 µm−1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the curvature analysis shown in the figure and supported by a citation.

claim: The fcpA– filament segments can be divided into two populations based on diameter.
source: The fcpA– filament segments can be divided into two populations, revealing a further correlation between sheath structure and filament curvature.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis.

claim: A 'thick' fcpA– segment population, whose estimated diameter (~170 Å) was consistent with the presence of a partial sheath, shows a propensity to form segments with curvature of ~3 µm−1.
source: A 'thick' fcpA– segment population, whose estimated diameter (~170 Å) was consistent with the presence of a partial sheath, shows a propensity to form segments with curvature of ~3 µm−1 (Figure 5C, blue bars).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the curvature analysis shown in the figure.

claim: A comparable number of 'thin' fcpA– segments, with an estimated diameter (~120 Å) indicative of an unsheathed core, shows a population shift towards lower curvature.
source: A comparable number of 'thin' fcpA– segments, with an estimated diameter (~120 Å) indicative of an unsheathed core, shows a population shift towards lower curvature (Figure 5C, orange bars).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the curvature analysis shown in the figure.

claim: An asymmetric subunit arrangement in the Leptospira flagellum is novel and previously unobserved either in exoflagellated bacteria or in other spirochetes.
source: Here we have identified a novel, asymmetric subunit arrangement in the Leptospira flagellum, previously unobserved either in exoflagellated bacteria or in other spirochetes.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the primary finding.

claim: The asymmetric architecture is functionally linked to flagellar supercoiling, a key attribute associated with spirochete motility.
source: We have further demonstrated that this asymmetric architecture is functionally linked to flagellar supercoiling, a key attribute associated with spirochete motility.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the primary finding.

claim: The means of controlling supercoiling in Leptospira contrasts with factors previously identified in other bacteria, which include changes in buffer composition (salt or pH) or the introduction of torsional strain due to flagellar rotation.
source: This means of controlling supercoiling contrasts with factors previously identified in other bacteria, which include changes in buffer composition (salt or pH) or the introduction of torsional strain due to flagellar rotation (Calladine et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by a citation.

claim: Earlier investigations of flagellar filament supercoiling have focused on exoflagellates, whose filaments are more simply constructed (homopolymers vs. the heteropolymer considered here).
source: However, earlier investigations of flagellar filament supercoiling have focused on exoflagellates, whose filaments are more simply constructed (homopolymers vs. the heteropolymer considered here), and whose functional roles differ in important ways from spirochete flagellar filaments.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work and its limitations.

claim: An important innovation in the current work was the application of a subtomogram averaging procedure to solve structures of the supercoiled form present in wild-type Leptospira flagellar filaments.
source: An important innovation in the current work was the application of a subtomogram averaging procedure to solve structures of the supercoiled form present in wild-type Leptospira flagellar filaments.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological innovation.

claim: Previous structural studies of flagellar filaments utilized mutant forms that strongly favor a straight, helically symmetric filament conformation, as was required for high-resolution cryo-EM analysis.
source: This approach contrasts with previous structural studies of flagellar filaments, most of which utilized mutant forms that strongly favor a straight, helically symmetric filament conformation, as was required for high-resolution cryo-EM analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work and its limitations.

claim: One prior study reports the structure of a supercoiled spirochete flagellum; however, in that case the filament was analyzed under the assumption of helical symmetry and was computationally straightened, obscuring any asymmetry.
source: One prior study reports the structure of a supercoiled spirochete flagellum (Liu et al., 2010); however, in that case the filament was analyzed under the assumption of helical symmetry and was computationally straightened, obscuring any asymmetry.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work and its limitations, supported by a citation.

claim: A supercoiled form of the Salmonella flagellar hook was resolved to near-atomic resolution by single-particle cryo-EM.
source: More recently, a supercoiled form of the Salmonella flagellar hook was resolved to near-atomic resolution by single-particle cryo-EM (Kato et al., 2019; Shibata et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The methods used to resolve the Salmonella flagellar hook are not well suited for all supercoil morphologies, particularly large-diameter supercoils that are unfavorably oriented within the specimen ice layer.
source: However, the methods used in these latter works are not well suited for all supercoil morphologies, particularly large-diameter supercoils (as in the current work) that are unfavorably oriented within the specimen ice layer.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior methods.

claim: The flattened supercoil shape observed in wild-type Leptospira sample is consistent with prior observations of these filaments.
source: The flattened supercoil shape observed in our wild-type Leptospira sample, while consistent with prior observations of these filaments (Wolgemuth et al., 2006), diverges from forms seen in other bacteria, including exoflagellates (Calladine, 1975; Calladine, 1976; Calladine et al., 2013; Fujii et al., 2008; Kamiya et al., 1980; Wolgemuth et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Functional exoflagella, including from Salmonella, interconvert between up to 12 distinct supercoil polymorphs.
source: Functional exoflagella, including from Salmonella, interconvert between up to 12 distinct supercoil polymorphs, but preferentially adopt an extended, left-handed supercoil form at rest or during smooth swimming ('Normal'; superhelical pitch and diameter of 2.66 and 0.6 µm, respectively).
evidence: This is a statement about prior knowledge of exoflagella.

claim: The left-handed, low-pitch geometry identified in wild-type Leptospira filaments more closely resembles an alternative exoflagella supercoil type that forms under low pH conditions ('Coiled'; superhelical pitch and diameter of ~0 and 1.0 µm, respectively).
source: The left-handed, low-pitch geometry we identify in wild-type Leptospira filaments (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) more closely resembles an alternative exoflagella supercoil type that forms under low pH conditions ('Coiled'; superhelical pitch and diameter of ~0 and 1.0 µm, respectively).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the data shown in the figure.

claim: The supercoil diameter in the Leptospira filament (0.45 µm) is less than half that of the 'Coiled' exoflagellar form.
source: However, the supercoil diameter in the Leptospira filament (0.45 µm) is less than half that of the 'Coiled' exoflagellar form.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data.

claim: Wild-type Leptospira filaments are much more curved (curvature is ~5 µm−1) than observed or predicted polymorphic forms from exoflagellates, which range in curvature from 0 ~ 3 µm−1.
source: Overall, wild-type Leptospira filaments are much more curved (curvature is ~5 µm−1; Figure 5A) than observed or predicted polymorphic forms from exoflagellates, which range in curvature from 0 ~ 3 µm−1 (Calladine, 1975; Kamiya and Asakura, 1976).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the data shown in the figure and supported by citations.

claim: Loss of sheath proteins reduces the curvature of Leptospira filaments, resulting in supercoiling geometries more consistent with the polymorphic forms observed in exoflagella.
source: Loss of sheath proteins reduces the curvature of Leptospira filaments, resulting in supercoiling geometries more consistent with the polymorphic forms observed in exoflagella.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: Despite their loss of curvature compared with wild-type filaments, fcpA– filaments remain markedly more curved than cryo-EM samples of tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) filaments or amyloid fibrils, which lack inherent supercoiling character.
source: Despite their loss of curvature compared with wild-type filaments (Figure 5A,C; Wunder et al., 2016a), fcpA– filaments remain markedly more curved than cryo-EM samples of tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) filaments or amyloid fibrils, which lack inherent supercoiling character.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the data shown in the figure and supported by a citation.

claim: For 'straight' TMV and amyloid filaments, an average curvature ~0.7 µm−1 was estimated from cryo-EM specimens.
source: For 'straight' TMV and amyloid filaments, an average curvature ~0.7 µm−1 was estimated from cryo-EM specimens (attributable to thermal fluctuations, variable fluid flow during sample preparation and other factors) (Rohou and Grigorieff, 2014), compared to values of up to ~3 µm−1 observed in the fcpA– sample (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Despite loss of most or all of the sheath, the 'thin' fcpA– population maintains an average curvature value (~2 µm−1) that exceeds that of straight TMV or amyloid filaments by more than a factor of two.
source: Despite loss of most or all of the sheath, the 'thin' fcpA– population maintains an average curvature value (~2 µm−1) that exceeds that of straight TMV or amyloid filaments by more than a factor of two (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data shown in the figure.

claim: The estimated curvature for bare Leptospira filament cores falls within the range observed in exoflagellar polymorphs (0–3 µm−1).
source: The estimated curvature for these bare Leptospira filament cores, falls within the range observed in exoflagellar polymorphs (0–3 µm−1) (Calladine, 1975).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by a citation.

claim: The Leptospira flagellar filament core may retain polymorphic, supercoiled behavior similar to exoflagellates.
source: This characteristic, as well as the occasional observation of 'wavy', sinusoidal fcpA– filaments of appropriate shape parameters (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), supports the idea that the Leptospira flagellar filament core may retain polymorphic, supercoiled behavior similar to exoflagellates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in the figure.

claim: Binding of Leptospira sheath proteins (particularly FcpA and FcpB) initiates an allosteric, cooperative transition of the core from a straighter form to the flattened, highly curved supercoil geometry suited for swimming.
source: Regardless of specific structural and functional core properties, our data indicate that binding of Leptospira sheath proteins (particularly FcpA and FcpB) initiates an allosteric, cooperative transition of the core from a straighter (but potentially polymorphic) form (Figure 5D,E), to the flattened, highly curved supercoil geometry suited for swimming (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in the figure.

claim: A potential mechanism for sheath-enforced curvature involves recognition by the sheath proteins of distinct core lattice geometries that occur on different sides of a supercoiled filament.
source: A potential mechanism involves recognition by the sheath proteins of distinct core lattice geometries that occur on different sides of a supercoiled filament.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: For Leptospira, the lattice differences between inner and outer curvature are quite substantial: for the given filament geometry (120 Å core diameter and ~0.45 µm superhelix diameter), the axial repeating distance is 3 Å longer on the filament outer curvature than the inner curvature.
source: For Leptospira, these lattice differences are quite substantial: for the given filament geometry (120 Å core diameter and ~0.45 µm superhelix diameter), the axial repeating distance is 3 Å longer on the filament outer curvature than the inner curvature.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the structural data.

claim: If FcpA preferentially binds to longitudinally expanded protofilaments on the outer curvature of a supercoil, and the core preferentially adopts a shorter longitudinal repeat distance, a helical symmetry mismatch will be generated and a specific supercoiled geometry can be stabilized.
source: Therefore, if FcpA preferentially binds to longitudinally expanded protofilaments on the outer curvature of a supercoil, and the core preferentially adopts a shorter longitudinal repeat distance, a helical symmetry mismatch will be generated and a specific supercoiled geometry can be stabilized (Figure 5F,G; Caspar, 1963; Klug, 1967).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural observations and supported by citations.

claim: Binding of an additional sheath component (e.g., FcpB) that is specifically matched to the expanded FcpA lattice would be ideally suited to further reinforce the supercoiling geometry.
source: In this type of mechanism, binding of an additional sheath component (e.g., FcpB) that is specifically matched to the expanded FcpA lattice would be ideally suited to further reinforce the supercoiling geometry, as is observed here (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: The asymmetric sheath would lock the core into a single, nondegenerate shape.
source: A noteworthy feature of the flagellar supercoiling mechanism presented in Figure 5 is that the asymmetric sheath would lock the core into a single, nondegenerate shape.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: A supercoiled, homopolymer flagellar filament can potentially interconvert between 11 equivalent conformations with identical shape parameters but different, rotated patterns of expansion and contraction in the 11 protofilaments.
source: In contrast, a supercoiled, homopolymer flagellar filament can potentially interconvert between 11 equivalent conformations with identical shape parameters but different, rotated patterns of expansion and contraction in the 11 protofilaments.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of homopolymer flagellar filaments based on prior knowledge.

claim: A supercoiled homopolymer flagellum could propagate a helical wave without rotating or equivalently, rotate without propagating a helical wave.
source: Thus, a supercoiled homopolymer flagellum could propagate a helical wave without rotating (Klug, 1967) or equivalently, rotate without propagating a helical wave
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of homopolymer flagellar filaments based on prior knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: An asymmetrically assembled heteropolymer flagellum as described for Leptospira would be unable to propagate a helical wave without rotating or rotate without propagating a helical wave.
source: an asymmetrically assembled heteropolymer flagellum as we describe for Leptospira would be unable to do so.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Physics modeling studies indicate that curved filament morphology and stiffness are critical for motility in Leptospira and spirochetes in general.
source: Physics modeling studies indicate that curved filament morphology and stiffness are critical for motility in Leptospira and spirochetes in general (Berg et al., 1978; Dombrowski et al., 2009; Kan and Wolgemuth, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both curved filament morphology and stiffness can be enforced via the addition of an asymmetric sheath surrounding the filament core.
source: Both of these properties can be enforced via the addition of an asymmetric sheath surrounding the filament core.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Spirochete endoflagella possess specialized reinforcements, including extra-large motors capable of exerting higher torques than conventional exoflagellar motors.
source: To support the large loads involved in driving whole-body undulations, spirochete endoflagella possess specialized reinforcements, including extra-large motors capable of exerting higher torques than conventional exoflagellar motors (Beeby et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Spirochete endoflagella possess unique hooks exhibiting covalent crosslinking between FlgE subunits.
source: To support the large loads involved in driving whole-body undulations, spirochete endoflagella possess specialized reinforcements, including extra-large motors capable of exerting higher torques than conventional exoflagellar motors (Beeby et al., 2016) and unique hooks exhibiting covalent crosslinking between FlgE subunits (Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Leptospira, alone among the known spirochetes, has only a single flagellum at each cell end.
source: Moreover, Leptospira, alone among the known spirochetes, has only a single flagellum at each cell end, whereas Borrelia, Treponema, and other species exhibit multiple copies per cell end (Charon et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: One function of the sheath elements FcpA and FcpB may be to reinforce the endoflagellum to allow for even higher torque loads required in the absence of additional, supporting flagella.
source: One function of the sheath elements FcpA and FcpB, to date found only in Leptospira, may therefore be to reinforce the endoflagellum to allow for even higher torque loads required in the absence of additional, supporting flagella (Trachtenberg et al., 1986; Trachtenberg et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a proposed function based on the structural observations and supported by citations.

claim: Images of fcpA– filaments indicate that the remaining sheath components are capable of asymmetric binding, and may do so preferentially on the concave side of the filament.
source: Although FcpA and FcpB play conspicuous roles in supercoiling, our images of fcpA– filaments indicate that the remaining sheath components are themselves capable of asymmetric binding, and may do so preferentially on the concave side of the filament (Figure 3; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Table 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in the figure and table.

claim: The remaining sheath proteins in fcpA– filaments include FlaA1 and FlaA2, although they are not currently able to be localized in the filament map.
source: These sheath proteins include FlaA1 and FlaA2, although we are not currently able to localize these in the filament map.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current analysis.

claim: Orthologs of Leptospira FlaA proteins are found in all spirochetes.
source: Orthologs of Leptospira FlaA proteins are found in all spirochetes (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the distribution of FlaA proteins supported by a table.

claim: Loss of FlaA has been shown to modify the diameter of spirochetal filaments.
source: Furthermore, loss of FlaA has been shown to modify the diameter (Li et al., 2000a) and superhelical pitch (Lambert et al., 2012) of spirochetal filaments.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Loss of FlaA has been shown to modify the superhelical pitch of spirochetal filaments.
source: Furthermore, loss of FlaA has been shown to modify the diameter (Li et al., 2000a) and superhelical pitch (Lambert et al., 2012) of spirochetal filaments.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Asymmetric arrangement of components in the sheath (and/or the core) may be a general feature that contributes to flagellar supercoiling and motility in spirochetes.
source: These observations raise the possibility that asymmetric arrangement of components in the sheath (and/or the core) may be a general feature that contributes to flagellar supercoiling and motility in spirochetes.
evidence: This is a proposed generalization based on the findings.
